Order polytopes of crown posets

Teemu Lundström Address: Department of Mathematics and Systems Analysis, Aalto University, Otakaari 1, 02150, Espoo, Finland Email address: teemu.lundstrom@aalto.fi and Leonardo Saud Maia Leite Address: Department of Mathematics, KTH Royal Institute of Technology, SE-100 44 Stockholm, Sweden Email address: lsml@kth.se
Abstract.

In the last decade, the order polytope of the zigzag poset has been thoroughly studied. A related poset, called crown poset, obtained by adding an extra cover relation between the endpoints of an even zigzag poset, is not so well understood. In this paper, we study the order polytopes of crown posets. We provide explicit formulas for their ff-polynomials, and show that the sequence of coefficients of each ff-polynomial is log-concave and asymptotically normal. We provide recursive formulas for their Ehrhart polynomial, giving a counterpart to formulas found in the zigzag case by Petersen–Zhuang (2025). We use these formulas to simplify a computation by Ferroni–Morales–Panova (2025) of the linear term of the order polynomial of these posets. Furthermore, we provide a combinatorial interpretation for the coefficients of the h∗h^{*}-polynomial in terms of the cyclic swap statistic on cyclically alternating permutations, which provides a circular version of a result by Coons–Sullivant (2023).

Key words and phrases: 
Crown poset, order polytope, ff-vector, Chebyshev polynomial, order polynomial, Ehrhart polynomial, zigzag poset, h∗h^{*}-vector, cyclically alternating permutation, cyclic swap, gamma-nonnegativity

1. Introduction

Order polytopes were introduced by Richard P. Stanley [27] as a geometric representation of partially ordered sets (posets). They play a significant role in combinatorial geometry, optimization, and algebraic combinatorics. The zigzag (or the fence) poset ZnZ_{n} on [n][n] is defined by the cover relations 1≺2≻3≺⋯≻n−1≺n1\prec 2\succ 3\prec\cdots\succ n-1\prec n if nn is even and 1≺2≻3≺⋯≺n−1≻n1\prec 2\succ 3\prec\cdots\prec n-1\succ n if nn is odd, see Figure 1, and it has been extensively studied in the literature [9, 23], but the same cannot be said about the crown poset. The crown poset 𝒞2​n\mathcal{C}_{2n} on [2​n][2n] is defined by the cover relations 1≺2≻3≺⋯≻2​n−1≺2​n≻11\prec 2\succ 3\prec\cdots\succ 2n-1\prec 2n\succ 1, that is, it corresponds to the zigzag poset Z2​nZ_{2n} with the extra cover relation 2​n≻12n\succ 1, see Figure 2.

In this paper we study the order polytope of the crown poset 𝒞2​n\mathcal{C}_{2n}. The crown poset 𝒞2​n\mathcal{C}_{2n} is the poset of proper faces of a polygon with nn vertices. The motivation for studying these posets came from studying order polytopes constructed from face lattices of more complicated polytopes. We will discuss this more in Section 6.

The following is an outline of the paper with our main results highlighted.

In Section 2, we quickly mention the relevant background related to order polytopes and Ehrhart theory, as well as fix some notation. In Section 3, we study the ff-polynomial of 𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n)\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{C}_{2n}): we provide an explicit formula for each of its coefficients, and use this to prove that these coefficients are a log-concave sequence and also asymptotically normal. These formulas are obtained by using the well-known connection between faces of the order polytope and the so called connected and compatible partitions of the underlying poset. We count these partitions using elementary combinatorial methods.

In Section 4, we study the Ehrhart polynomial of 𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n)\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{C}_{2n}). We provide a recursive formula for the order polynomial of 𝒞2​n\mathcal{C}_{2n} in terms of order polynomials of zigzags, which gives a recursive expression for the Ehrhart polynomial of 𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n)\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{C}_{2n}). This provides a counterpart to the formulas found in the zigzag case in [23]. This also allows us to simplify the computation for the linear coefficient of the order polynomial Ω𝒞2​n​(t)\Omega_{\mathcal{C}_{2n}}(t) made in [11].

2. Preliminaries

In this section we quickly give some conventions and notation used in this paper. We mostly follow standard terminology from polytope theory and Ehrhart theory (see e.g. [1]).

We consider the empty set ∅\emptyset as a face of a polytope of dimension −1-1. The full polytope is also considered to be a face. The ff-vector of a dd-polytope 𝔭\mathfrak{p} is denoted by f⁡(𝔭)=(f−1​(𝔭),f0​(𝔭)​…,fd​(𝔭))f(\mathfrak{p})=(f_{-1}(\mathfrak{p}),f_{0}(\mathfrak{p})\dots,f_{d}(\mathfrak{p})), where fi​(𝔭)f_{i}(\mathfrak{p}) is the number of ii-dimensional faces of 𝔭\mathfrak{p}, and the ff-polynomial f𝔭​(t)f_{\mathfrak{p}}(t) of 𝔭\mathfrak{p} is the generating polynomial of f⁡(𝔭)f(\mathfrak{p}), that is, f𝔭​(t)=∑i=0d+1fi−1​(𝔭)​tif_{\mathfrak{p}}(t)=\sum_{i=0}^{d+1}f_{i-1}(\mathfrak{p})t^{i}. If 𝔭⊆ℝd\mathfrak{p}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} is a lattice polytope then the integer point counting function k↦#⁡(k​𝔭∩ℤd):ℤ>0→ℤ≥0k\mapsto\#(k\mathfrak{p}\cap\mathbb{Z}^{d})\colon\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\to\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} agrees with a polynomial, called the Ehrhart polynomial, which we denote by L⁡(𝔭,k)L(\mathfrak{p},k). The series 1+∑k≥1L⁡(𝔭,k)​tk1+\sum_{k\geq 1}L(\mathfrak{p},k)t^{k} can be written as a rational function

1+∑k≥1L⁡(𝔭,k)​tk=h0∗​(𝔭)+h1∗​(𝔭)​t+⋯+hd∗​(𝔭)​td(1−t)d+11+\sum_{k\geq 1}L(\mathfrak{p},k)t^{k}=\dfrac{h_{0}^{*}(\mathfrak{p})+h_{1}^{*}(\mathfrak{p})t+\cdots+h_{d}^{*}(\mathfrak{p})t^{d}}{(1-t)^{d+1}}

where the polynomial h𝔭∗​(t)=h0∗​(𝔭)+h1∗​(𝔭)​t+⋯+hd∗​(𝔭)​tdh_{\mathfrak{p}}^{*}(t)=h_{0}^{*}(\mathfrak{p})+h_{1}^{*}(\mathfrak{p})t+\cdots+h_{d}^{*}(\mathfrak{p})t^{d} is called the h∗h^{*}-polynomial of 𝔭\mathfrak{p}, and the vector h∗​(𝔭)=(h0∗​(𝔭),h1∗​(𝔭),…,hd∗​(𝔭))h^{*}(\mathfrak{p})=(h_{0}^{*}(\mathfrak{p}),h_{1}^{*}(\mathfrak{p}),\ldots,h_{d}^{*}(\mathfrak{p})) is the h∗h^{*}-vector of 𝔭\mathfrak{p}.

Next, we quickly recall basic facts about order polytopes. For more on order polytopes see [27]. Let P=([d],⪯)P=([d],\preceq) be a finite poset. The order polytope 𝒪⁡(P)\mathcal{O}(P) is the polytope

{x=(x1,…,xd)∈[0,1]d∣xi≤xj​ for all ​i⪯j​ in ​P}.\{x=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{d})\in[0,1]^{d}\mid x_{i}\leq x_{j}\text{ for all }i\preceq j\text{ in }P\}.

These are full-dimensional polytopes, that is, dim(𝒪⁡(P))=|P|\dim(\mathcal{O}(P))=|P|. The vertices of 𝒪⁡(P)\mathcal{O}(P) are in bijection with the indicator vectors of filters of PP and the facet-defining inequalities of 𝒪⁡(P)\mathcal{O}(P) are given by

0≤xi\displaystyle 0\leq x_{i}   for all ii minimal
xj≤1\displaystyle x_{j}\leq 1   for all jj maximal
xi≤xj\displaystyle x_{i}\leq x_{j}   for all cover relations i≺ji\prec j .

Order polytopes also admit unimodular triangulations, which are constructed as follows: let σ\sigma be a linear extension of PP, and let v0σ=∑i=1deiv_{0}^{\sigma}=\sum_{i=1}^{d}e_{i}. Recursively define viσv_{i}^{\sigma} to be viσ=vi−1σ−eσ−1​(i)v_{i}^{\sigma}=v_{i-1}^{\sigma}-e_{\sigma^{-1}(i)} and then define Δσ\Delta^{\sigma} to be the convex hull of v0σ,v1σ,…,vdσv_{0}^{\sigma},v_{1}^{\sigma},\ldots,v_{d}^{\sigma}. Then the simplices Δσ\Delta^{\sigma} corresponding to all linear extensions σ\sigma of PP form a unimodular triangulation of 𝒪⁡(P)\mathcal{O}(P) which we will refer to as the canonical triangulation.

3. The ff-polynomial of 𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n)\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{C}_{2n})

We start by studying the ff-polynomial of 𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n)\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{C}_{2n}). Since 𝒞2​n\mathcal{C}_{2n} has nn minimal elements, nn maximal elements and 2​n2n cover relations, it follows that 𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n)\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{C}_{2n}) has 4​n4n facets. In fact, we can compute explicitly each entry of the ff-polynomial of 𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n)\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{C}_{2n}). We will approach this by using the well-known characterization of faces of order polytopes in terms of so called connected and compatible partitions of the underlying poset. We begin by reviewing the related terminology.

Fix a finite poset PP and let π={B1,…,Bk}\pi=\{B_{1},\dots,B_{k}\} be a partition of the ground set of PP. We call the sets BiB_{i} either parts or blocks. We say that π\pi is connected if each BiB_{i}, considered as an induced subposet, is connected. Recall that a poset is connected if its comparability graph is connected. We introduce an order relation ≤π\leq_{\pi} on the blocks of π\pi by setting Bi≤πBjB_{i}\leq_{\pi}B_{j} if there is some x∈Bix\in B_{i} and y∈Bjy\in B_{j} such that x≤yx\leq y in PP. Note that ≤π\leq_{\pi} is reflexive but not necessarily transitive or antisymmetric. If the transitive closure of ≤π\leq_{\pi} is antisymmetric, we say π\pi is compatible. Note that the transitive closure of ≤π\leq_{\pi} is antisymmetric if and only if for all blocks of π\pi

Bi≤π⋯≤πBj≤π⋯≤πBi implies Bi=Bj.B_{i}\leq_{\pi}\dots\leq_{\pi}B_{j}\leq_{\pi}\dots\leq_{\pi}B_{i}\quad\text{ implies }B_{i}=B_{j}.

A sequence of blocks of the form Bi≤π⋯≤πBj≤π⋯≤πBiB_{i}\leq_{\pi}\dots\leq_{\pi}B_{j}\leq_{\pi}\dots\leq_{\pi}B_{i} is called a cycle. Hence, π\pi is compatible if and only if there are no cycles among the blocks of π\pi, other than cycles consisting of a single block. We often write just ≤\leq instead of ≤π\leq_{\pi}. If π\pi is a connected and compatible partition we call π\pi a CCP for short. If |π|=k|\pi|=k and π\pi is a CCP we call π\pi a kk-CCP.

The faces of 𝒪⁡(P)\mathcal{O}(P) turn out to correspond to, not CCPs of PP, but CCPs of P^=P∪{0^,1^}\hat{P}=P\cup\{\hat{0},\hat{1}\}, which is the poset obtained from PP by adding a minimum element 0^\hat{0} and a maximum element 1^\hat{1}.

Theorem 3.1 ([27]).

Let PP be a finite poset of size dd. Let 0≤k≤d0\leq k\leq d. The kk-faces of 𝒪⁡(P)\mathcal{O}(P) are in bijection with the (k+2)(k+2)-CCPs of P^\hat{P}.

We turn to studying CCPs of 𝒞2​n\mathcal{C}_{2n} and 𝒞^2​n\hat{\mathcal{C}}_{2n}. The CCPs of 𝒞2​n\mathcal{C}_{2n} are easy to recognize:

Lemma 3.2.

A connected partition of 𝒞2​n\mathcal{C}_{2n} with at least two blocks is compatible if and only if at least one block has odd cardinality.

Proof.

First, suppose π\pi is a connected partition of 𝒞2​n\mathcal{C}_{2n}. Write the elements of 𝒞2​n\mathcal{C}_{2n} as

(∗\ast) a1<b1>a2<b2>⋯<bn>a1.a_{1}<b_{1}>a_{2}<b_{2}>\cdots<b_{n}>a_{1}.

Since each block of π\pi is connected, each block is going to consist of (cyclically) consecutive elements in the list (∗)(\ast). If B≤B′B\leq B^{\prime} for some B,B′∈πB,B^{\prime}\in\pi and B≠B′B\neq B^{\prime} then there needs to be elements a∈Ba\in B and b∈B′b\in B^{\prime} that are (cyclically) consecutive in the list (∗)(\ast). Hence the only way to have B≤B′B\leq B^{\prime} for two distinct blocks is if the union B∪B′B\cup B^{\prime} consists of (cyclically) consecutive elements. Thus, if there are any cycles among the blocks of π\pi, any element in 𝒞2​n\mathcal{C}_{2n} is going to appear in one of those blocks. Therefore, any cycle among the blocks of π\pi is going to contain all blocks.

With this observation we now fix a connected partition π={B1,…,Bk}\pi=\{B_{1},\dots,B_{k}\} of 𝒞2​n\mathcal{C}_{2n} where k≥2k\geq 2 and proceed to prove the lemma.

Suppose π\pi has an odd block BiB_{i}. Either BiB_{i} is of the form

Bi={ai1<bi2>⋯<bim>aim+1}B_{i}=\{a_{i_{1}}<b_{i_{2}}>\cdots<b_{i_{m}}>a_{i_{m+1}}\}

or BiB_{i} is of the form

Bi={bi1>ai2<⋯>aim<bim+1}.B_{i}=\{b_{i_{1}}>a_{i_{2}}<\cdots>a_{i_{m}}<b_{i_{m+1}}\}.

In the first case there cannot be any block Bj≠BiB_{j}\neq B_{i} with Bj≤BiB_{j}\leq B_{i}. In the second case there cannot be any block Bj≠BiB_{j}\neq B_{i} with Bi≤BjB_{i}\leq B_{j}. Hence BiB_{i} cannot appear in any non-trivial cycle. We conclude that π\pi is compatible.

Then suppose every block of π\pi has even cardinality. We aim to show that π\pi is not compatible. Now either each BiB_{i} is of the form

Bi={ai1<bi2>⋯>aim<bim+1}B_{i}=\{a_{i_{1}}<b_{i_{2}}>\cdots>a_{i_{m}}<b_{i_{m+1}}\}

or each BiB_{i} is of the form

Bi={bi1>ai2<⋯<bim>aim+1}.B_{i}=\{b_{i_{1}}>a_{i_{2}}<\cdots<b_{i_{m}}>a_{i_{m+1}}\}.

Hence we can chain together all the blocks of π\pi to form a cycle B1≤B2≤⋯≤Bk≤B1B_{1}\leq B_{2}\leq\dots\leq B_{k}\leq B_{1}. Since k≥2k\geq 2, we conclude that π\pi is not compatible. ∎

The comparability graph of 𝒞2​n\mathcal{C}_{2n} is the cycle graph on 2​n2n elements. By Lemma 3.2, the CCPs of 𝒞2​n\mathcal{C}_{2n} therefore correspond to connected partitions of the vertex set of the cycle graph where at least one part has odd cardinality. Counting such partitions seems combinatorially feasible. However, the faces of 𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n)\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{C}_{2n}) do not correspond to CCPs of 𝒞2​n\mathcal{C}_{2n} but instead to the CCPs of 𝒞^2​n=𝒞2​n∪{0^,1^}\hat{\mathcal{C}}_{2n}=\mathcal{C}_{2n}\cup\{\hat{0},\hat{1}\}. The next proposition shows how to obtain the CCPs of 𝒞^2​n\hat{\mathcal{C}}_{2n} from the CCPs of 𝒞2​n\mathcal{C}_{2n}.

Proposition 3.3.

For all k≥2k\geq 2 let

𝒜k={(P,S):P is a CCP of 𝒞2​n,S⊆{odd parts of P},|P|−|S|=k−2}.\mathcal{A}_{k}=\{(P,S)\colon P\text{ is a CCP of }\mathcal{C}_{2n},\ S\subseteq\{\text{odd parts of }P\},\ |P|-|S|=k-2\}.
  1. (i)

    For all k≥2k\geq 2 there is an injection 𝒜k⟶{k-CCP’s of ​𝒞^2​n}\mathcal{A}_{k}\longrightarrow\{\text{$k$-CCP's of }\hat{\mathcal{C}}_{2n}\}.

  2. (ii)

    For all k≥3k\geq 3 the injection is also surjective and thus

    #⁡{k-CCP’s of ​𝒞^2​n}=|𝒜k|.\#\{\text{$k$-CCP's of }\hat{\mathcal{C}}_{2n}\}=|\mathcal{A}_{k}|.
  3. (iii)

    For k=2k=2 the injection misses two elements and thus

    #⁡{2-CCP’s of ​𝒞^2​n}=|𝒜2|+2.\#\{\text{2-CCP's of }\hat{\mathcal{C}}_{2n}\}=|\mathcal{A}_{2}|+2.
Proof.

Let k≥2k\geq 2. Given a pair (P,S)∈𝒜k(P,S)\in\mathcal{A}_{k} we let S0={B1,…,Bm}⊆SS_{0}=\{B_{1},\dots,B_{m}\}\subseteq S be the set of parts in SS that have more lower elements than upper elements and S1={D1,…,Dℓ}⊆SS_{1}=\{D_{1},\dots,D_{\ell}\}\subseteq S be the set of parts that have more upper elements than lower elements. Here S=S0⊔S1S=S_{0}\sqcup S_{1}. We map (P,S)(P,S) to

π=(P∖S)∪{B1∪⋯∪Bm∪{0^}}∪{D1∪⋯∪Dℓ∪{1^}},\pi=(P\setminus S)\cup\{B_{1}\cup\dots\cup B_{m}\cup\{\hat{0}\}\}\cup\{D_{1}\cup\dots\cup D_{\ell}\cup\{\hat{1}\}\},

see Figure 3. Our aim is to show that this mapping is a well-defined injection 𝒜k→{k-CCP’s of ​𝒞^2​n}.\mathcal{A}_{k}\to\{\text{$k$-CCP's of }\hat{\mathcal{C}}_{2n}\}. First we show that this map is well-defined. Use the same notation as above. Our aim is to show that π\pi is a kk-CCP of 𝒞^2​n\hat{\mathcal{C}}_{2n}. Since PP is a partition of 𝒞2​n\mathcal{C}_{2n}, it is easy to see that π\pi is a partition of 𝒞^2​n\hat{\mathcal{C}}_{2n}. The parts in P∖SP\setminus S are connected since PP was connected, and the new parts B1∪⋯∪Bm∪{0^}B_{1}\cup\dots\cup B_{m}\cup\{\hat{0}\} and D1∪⋯∪Dℓ∪{1^}D_{1}\cup\dots\cup D_{\ell}\cup\{\hat{1}\} are clearly connected. Here |π|=|P|−|S|+2=k|\pi|=|P|-|S|+2=k. It remains to show that π\pi is compatible. Since each BiB_{i} is connected and has more lower elements than upper elements, each BiB_{i} looks something like in Figure 4(a). Similarly, since each DiD_{i} is connected and has more upper elements than lower elements, each DiD_{i} looks something like in Figure 4(b). In particular, no part of PP can be below any BiB_{i}, and no part of PP can be above any DiD_{i}. Write P∖S={C1,…,Cr}P\setminus S=\{C_{1},\dots,C_{r}\}. Furthermore, write B=B1∪⋯∪Bm∪{0^}B=B_{1}\cup\dots\cup B_{m}\cup\{\hat{0}\} and D=D1∪⋯∪Dℓ∪{1^}D=D_{1}\cup\dots\cup D_{\ell}\cup\{\hat{1}\}. Thus π={C1,…,Cr,B,D}\pi=\{C_{1},\dots,C_{r},B,D\}. where

We finish this section by finding another expression for the number of vertices of 𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n)\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{C}_{2n}). Recall that the Lucas sequence is an integer sequence defined recursively by L⁡(0)=2L(0)=2, L⁡(1)=1L(1)=1, and L⁡(n)=L⁡(n−1)+L⁡(n−2)L(n)=L(n-1)+L(n-2) if n>1n>1. It is closely related to the cycle graph OnO_{n} since it corresponds to the number of matchings and to the number of independent vertex sets and vertex covers of OnO_{n} for n≥3n\geq 3 [22, A000032]. From this we deduce:

Corollary 3.7.

The number of vertices of 𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n)\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{C}_{2n}) is L⁡(2​n)L(2n). In particular, for every n≥0n\geq 0,

L⁡(2​n)=(1+52)2​n+(1−52)2​n=2+∑i=22​n∑m=1⌊i/2⌋2​ni​(i2​m)​(n+m−1i−1)​(2​mi).L(2n)=\left(\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}\right)^{2n}+\left(\frac{1-\sqrt{5}}{2}\right)^{2n}=2+\sum_{i=2}^{2n}\sum_{m=1}^{\lfloor i/2\rfloor}\frac{2n}{i}\binom{i}{2m}\binom{n+m-1}{i-1}\binom{2m}{i}\quad.
Proof.

The first equality is well-known and follows from the definition of Lucas sequence. For the second equality, observe that the number of vertices in an order polytope of a poset PP is the number of filters in PP, which equals the number of antichains in PP. Hence, it suffices to compute the number of antichains in 𝒞2​n\mathcal{C}_{2n}. The Hasse diagram of 𝒞2​n\mathcal{C}_{2n} as a graph is also its own comparability graph. Since the number of independent sets in a comparability graph of a poset is the number of antichains in that poset, there are L⁡(2​n)L(2n) antichains in 𝒞2​n\mathcal{C}_{2n}. The formula now follows from Theorem 3.6 using k=0k=0. ∎

3.1. The log-concavity of the ff-vector

Let 𝒮={ak}k=0n\mathcal{S}=\{a_{k}\}_{k=0}^{n} be a sequence of real numbers. We say that

  • •

    𝒮\mathcal{S} is unimodal if there exists 0≤m≤n0\leq m\leq n such that a0≤⋯≤am−1≤am≥am+1≥⋯≥ana_{0}\leq\cdots\leq a_{m-1}\leq a_{m}\geq a_{m+1}\geq\cdots\geq a_{n};

  • •

    𝒮\mathcal{S} is log-concave if ak2≥ak+1​ak−1a_{k}^{2}\geq a_{k+1}a_{k-1} for all k=1,…,n−1k=1,\ldots,n-1;

  • •

    𝒮\mathcal{S} is ultra log-concave if {ak/(nk)}k=0n\left\{\nicefrac{{a_{k}}}{{\binom{n}{k}}}\right\}_{k=0}^{n} is log-concave;

  • •

    the generating polynomial of 𝒮\mathcal{S}, p𝒮​(t)=a0+a1​t+…​an​tnp_{\mathcal{S}}(t)=a_{0}+a_{1}t+\ldots a_{n}t^{n}, is real-rooted if p𝒮​(t)p_{\mathcal{S}}(t) has only real-roots.

The following classical lemma connects the four properties above:

Lemma 3.8.

Let 𝒮={ak}k=0n\mathcal{S}=\{a_{k}\}_{k=0}^{n} be a sequence of nonnegative real numbers. If

  1. (i)

    p𝒮​(t)p_{\mathcal{S}}(t) is real-rooted, then 𝒮\mathcal{S} is ultra log-concave;

  2. (ii)

    𝒮\mathcal{S} is ultra log-concave, then 𝒮\mathcal{S} is log-concave;

  3. (iii)

    𝒮\mathcal{S} is log-concave and ak>0a_{k}>0 for all k=0,1,…,nk=0,1,\ldots,n, then 𝒮\mathcal{S} is unimodal.

In this section, we prove the log-concavity of the entries of the ff-vector of 𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n)\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{C}_{2n}). The following simple lemma will be useful in the proof of Theorem 3.12:

Lemma 3.9.

Let b0,b1≥0b_{0},b_{1}\geq 0. If 𝒮={ak}k=0n\mathcal{S}=\{a_{k}\}_{k=0}^{n} is a ultra log-concave sequence of nonnegative real numbers such that a0≥b0a_{0}\geq b_{0}, a1≥2​b1a_{1}\geq 2b_{1}, then {a0+b0,a1+b1,a2,…,an}\{a_{0}+b_{0},a_{1}+b_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{n}\} is a log-concave sequence.

Proof.

By Lemma 3.8(ii), it is sufficient to show that

(3.4) (a1+b1)2≥(a0+b0)⋅a2(a_{1}+b_{1})^{2}\geq(a_{0}+b_{0})\cdot a_{2}

and

(3.5) a22≥(a1+b1)⋅a3.a_{2}^{2}\geq(a_{1}+b_{1})\cdot a_{3}.

a12(n1)2≥a0(n0)⋅a2(n2)⟹a12≥2​nn−1​a0​a2≥2​a0​a2.\frac{a_{1}^{2}}{\binom{n}{1}^{2}}\geq\frac{a_{0}}{\binom{n}{0}}\cdot\frac{a_{2}}{\binom{n}{2}}\implies a_{1}^{2}\geq\frac{2n}{n-1}a_{0}a_{2}\geq 2a_{0}a_{2}.

Hence,

(a0+b0)⋅a2>(a1+b1)2≥2​a0​a2+2​a1​b1+b12⟹ .\displaystyle(a_{0}+b_{0})\cdot a_{2}>(a_{1}+b_{1})^{2}\geq 2a_{0}a_{2}+2a_{1}b_{1}+b_{1}^{2}\implies\smash{\text{\quad\raisebox{-8.39996pt}{.}}}

By hypothesis, a0≥b0a_{0}\geq b_{0}, from which follows that 0≥a2>2​a1​b1+b120\geq a_{2}>2a_{1}b_{1}+b_{1}^{2}, which is a contradiction because a1,b1≥0a_{1},b_{1}\geq 0. Therefore, (3.4) holds.

Now, suppose that (3.5) does not hold, that is, (a1+b1)⋅a3>a22(a_{1}+b_{1})\cdot a_{3}>a_{2}^{2}. Again, by ultra log-concavity of 𝒮\mathcal{S},

a22(n2)2≥a1(n1)⋅a3(n3)⟹a22≥3​(n−1)2​(n−2)​a1​a3≥32​a1​a3.\frac{a_{2}^{2}}{\binom{n}{2}^{2}}\geq\frac{a_{1}}{\binom{n}{1}}\cdot\frac{a_{3}}{\binom{n}{3}}\implies a_{2}^{2}\geq\frac{3(n-1)}{2(n-2)}a_{1}a_{3}\geq\frac{3}{2}a_{1}a_{3}.

0>a3​(a12−b1)\displaystyle 0>a_{3}\left(\frac{a_{1}}{2}-b_{1}\right)

which is a contradiction, since a1≥2​b1a_{1}\geq 2b_{1} implies a3​(a12−b1)≥0a_{3}\left(\frac{a_{1}}{2}-b_{1}\right)\geq 0. Therefore, (3.5) holds. ∎

The next result will not be used throughout this paper, but it can be seen as a generalization of Lemma 3.9:

Proposition 3.10.

Let 𝒮={ak}k=0n\mathcal{S}=\{a_{k}\}_{k=0}^{n} and 𝒯={bk}k=0n\mathcal{T}=\{b_{k}\}_{k=0}^{n} be sequences of nonnegative real numbers such that 𝒮\mathcal{S} is ultra log-concave and 𝒯\mathcal{T} is log-concave. If ak≥2​(k+1)⋅bka_{k}\geq 2(k+1)\cdot b_{k} for all k∈{0,1,…,n}k\in\{0,1,\ldots,n\}, then 𝒰={ak+bk}k=0n\mathcal{U}=\{a_{k}+b_{k}\}_{k=0}^{n} is a log-concave sequence.

ai2(ni)2≥ai−1(ni−1)⋅ai+1(ni+1)⟹ai2≥i+1i​n−i+1n−i​ai−1​ai+1≥i+1i​ai−1​ai+1.\frac{a_{i}^{2}}{\binom{n}{i}^{2}}\geq\frac{a_{i-1}}{\binom{n}{i-1}}\cdot\frac{a_{i+1}}{\binom{n}{i+1}}\implies a_{i}^{2}\geq\frac{i+1}{i}\frac{n-i+1}{n-i}a_{i-1}a_{i+1}\geq\frac{i+1}{i}a_{i-1}a_{i+1}.

Hence,

(ai−1+bi−1)⋅(ai+1+bi+1)>(ai+bi)2≥i+1i​ai−1​ai+1+2​ai​bi+bi2⟹ .\displaystyle(a_{i-1}+b_{i-1})\cdot(a_{i+1}+b_{i+1})>(a_{i}+b_{i})^{2}\geq\frac{i+1}{i}a_{i-1}a_{i+1}+2a_{i}b_{i}+b_{i}^{2}\implies\smash{\text{\quad\raisebox{-8.39996pt}{.}}}
(3.7) ai+1​(bi−1−ai−12​i)+ai−1​(bi+1−ai+12​i)>2​ai​bi+(bi2−bi−1​bi+1)\displaystyle a_{i+1}\left(b_{i-1}-\frac{a_{i-1}}{2i}\right)+a_{i-1}\left(b_{i+1}-\frac{a_{i+1}}{2i}\right)>2a_{i}b_{i}+(b_{i}^{2}-b_{i-1}b_{i+1})

0>2​ai​bi+(bi2−bi−1​bi+1).0>2a_{i}b_{i}+(b_{i}^{2}-b_{i-1}b_{i+1}).

However, this is a contradiction since ai,bi≥0a_{i},b_{i}\geq 0 and 𝒯\mathcal{T} is log-concave. Therefore, the proposition follows. ∎

Remark 3.11.

Neither Lemma 3.9 nor Proposition 3.10 holds true if we try to prove that the new sequence obtained is ultra log-concave. In fact, take 𝒮1={1/10,2,2,1,1/10,1/250}\mathcal{S}_{1}=\{1/10,2,2,1,1/10,1/250\} and 𝒯1={0,1,0,0,0,0}\mathcal{T}_{1}=\{0,1,0,0,0,0\}. Then 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} is ultra log-concave and 𝒯1\mathcal{T}_{1} is log-concave, but the sequence 𝒰1={1/10,3,2,1,1/10,1/250}\mathcal{U}_{1}=\{1/10,3,2,1,1/10,1/250\} is not ultra log-concave since

(2(52))2<3(51)⋅1(53).\left(\frac{2}{\binom{5}{2}}\right)^{2}<\frac{3}{\binom{5}{1}}\cdot\frac{1}{\binom{5}{3}}.

Another counterexample is 𝒮2={1,4,3,1,1/10,1/250}\mathcal{S}_{2}=\{1,4,3,1,1/10,1/250\} and 𝒯2={1,1,0,0,0,0}\mathcal{T}_{2}=\{1,1,0,0,0,0\}. Again, 𝒮2\mathcal{S}_{2} is ultra log-concave and 𝒯2\mathcal{T}_{2} is log-concave, but 𝒰2={2,5,3,1,1/10,1/250}\mathcal{U}_{2}=\{2,5,3,1,1/10,1/250\} is not ultra log-concave since

(3(52))2<5(51)⋅1(53).\left(\frac{3}{\binom{5}{2}}\right)^{2}<\frac{5}{\binom{5}{1}}\cdot\frac{1}{\binom{5}{3}}.

Table 1 presents the ff-vectors of 𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n)\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{C}_{2n}) for small values of nn. Using a computer, it is easy to verify that f⁡(𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n))f(\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{C}_{2n})) is log-concave for large values of nn. The next result, which was independently proved by Hai-Ling Li, Shi-Mei Ma, and Ze-Chao Qu in [liface], shows that this is not just a coincidence:

Theorem 3.12.

For all n≥2n\geq 2, the entries of the ff-vector of 𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n)\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{C}_{2n}) form a log-concave sequence.

We need an additional result to prove Corollary 3.12. The Chebyshev polynomials of first kind Tn​(t)T_{n}(t) [21] are defined by the recurrence relation

Tn​(t)≔{1 if ​n=0t if ​n=12​t⋅Tn−1​(t)−Tn−2​(t) if ​n>1T_{n}(t)\coloneqq\begin{cases}1&\mbox{ if }n=0\\ t&\mbox{ if }n=1\\ 2t\cdot T_{n-1}(t)-T_{n-2}(t)&\mbox{ if }n>1\end{cases}

and its closed formula is

(3.8) Tn​(t)=n​∑m=0n(−2)m​(n+m−1)!(n−m)!⋅(2​m)!​(1−t)m=(t+t2−1)n+(t−t2−1)n2.T_{n}(t)=n\sum_{m=0}^{n}(-2)^{m}\frac{(n+m-1)!}{(n-m)!\cdot(2m)!}(1-t)^{m}=\frac{(t+\sqrt{t^{2}-1})^{n}+(t-\sqrt{t^{2}-1})^{n}}{2}\quad.

The Chebyshev polynomials of second kind Un​(t)U_{n}(t) are defined by the recurrence relation

Un​(t)≔{1 if ​n=02​t if ​n=12​t⋅Tn−1​(t)−Tn−2​(t) if ​n>1U_{n}(t)\coloneqq\begin{cases}1&\mbox{ if }n=0\\ 2t&\mbox{ if }n=1\\ 2t\cdot T_{n-1}(t)-T_{n-2}(t)&\mbox{ if }n>1\end{cases}

and its closed formula is

(3.9) Un​(t)=∑m=0n(−2)m​(n+m+1)!(n−m)!⋅(2​m+1)!​(1−t)m=(t+t2−1)n+1−(t−t2−1)n+12​t2−1.U_{n}(t)=\sum_{m=0}^{n}(-2)^{m}\frac{(n+m+1)!}{(n-m)!\cdot(2m+1)!}(1-t)^{m}=\frac{(t+\sqrt{t^{2}-1})^{n+1}-(t-\sqrt{t^{2}-1})^{n+1}}{2\sqrt{t^{2}-1}}\quad.

We now list some properties of Chebyshev polynomials. The Chebyshev polynomials of first and second kinds are related by the following expression:

(3.10) Tn′​(t)=n⋅Un−1​(t)for every ​n≥1.T_{n}^{\prime}(t)=n\cdot U_{n-1}(t)\quad\mbox{for every }n\geq 1.

The Chebyshev polynomials of first and second kinds are real-rooted [21, Chapter 2.2]. Moreover, on the interval [−1,1][-1,1], all of the extrema of Tn​(t)T_{n}(t) have values that are either −1-1 or 11 for all n≥1n\geq 1. More specifically, let d>2d>2 and k>0k>0 be such that d|2​nd\mid 2n, 0<k<d/20<k<d/2 and gcd⁡(k,d)=1\gcd(k,d)=1. Then,

  • •

    for even nn, Tn​(t)=1T_{n}(t)=1 if and only if t=±1t=\pm 1 or t=cos⁡(2​k​πd)t=\cos\left(\frac{2k\pi}{d}\right), with 2​nd\frac{2n}{d} even, and Tn​(t)=−1T_{n}(t)=-1 if and only if t=cos⁡(2​k​πd)t=\cos\left(\frac{2k\pi}{d}\right), with 2​nd\frac{2n}{d} odd, from which follows that there are n/2+1n/2+1 such values of tt;

    for odd nn, Tn​(t)=1T_{n}(t)=1 if and only if t=1t=1 or t=cos⁡(2​k​πd)t=\cos\left(\frac{2k\pi}{d}\right), with 2​nd\frac{2n}{d} even, and Tn​(t)=−1T_{n}(t)=-1 if and only if t=cos⁡(2​k​πd)t=\cos\left(\frac{2k\pi}{d}\right), with 2​nd\frac{2n}{d} odd, from which follows that there are (n+1)/2(n+1)/2 such values of tt.

3.2. A probabilistic result: the Central Limit Theorem for the ff-vector

Let a0,…,an≥0a_{0},\ldots,a_{n}\geq 0 be such that ∑k=0n(ak)=1\sum_{k=0}^{n}(a_{k})=1, and let XX be a discrete random variable taking values in {0,1,…,n}\{0,1,\ldots,n\} such that ℙ⁡(X=k)=ak\mathbb{P}(X=k)=a_{k} for all k=0,1,…,nk=0,1,\ldots,n. σX2=Var⁡(X)=𝔼⁡(X2)−[𝔼⁡(X)]2=pX′′​(1)+pX′​(1)−[pX′​(1)]2.\sigma^{2}_{X}=\mathrm{Var}(X)=\mathbb{E}(X^{2})-[\mathbb{E}(X)]^{2}=p_{X}^{\prime\prime}(1)+p_{X}^{\prime}(1)-[p_{X}^{\prime}(1)]^{2}.

The following result connects the theory of real-rooted polynomials and Probability Theory, and has been used to prove asymptotic normality of many sequences in Combinatorics, see e.g. [3, 4, 5, 17, 20].

Theorem 3.14.

Then

Xn−μXnσXn→𝐷N⁡(0,1)whenn→∞.\frac{X_{n}-\mu_{X_{n}}}{\sigma_{X_{n}}}\xrightarrow{D}N(0,1)\quad\mbox{when}\quad n\to\infty.

Equivalently, following Bender [3, Equation (1.1)(1.1)], {an,k}n,k≥0\{a_{n,k}\}_{n,k\geq 0} (or {Xn}n≥0\{X_{n}\}_{n\geq 0}) are asymptotically normal if and only if

4. The Ehrhart polynomial of 𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n)\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{C}_{2n})

In this section, we study the order polynomial of 𝒞2​n\mathcal{C}_{2n}. We present a recursive formula to compute Ω𝒞2​n​(t)\Omega_{\mathcal{C}_{2n}}(t) in terms of the order polynomials of zigzags. We use this recursion to give an alternative proof for the nonnegativity of the coefficients of Ω𝒞2​n​(t)\Omega_{\mathcal{C}_{2n}}(t), recently proved by Ferroni, Morales and Panova [11].

Given a finite poset PP, let ΩP:ℝ→ℝ\Omega_{P}\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R} be the function such that ΩP​(n)\Omega_{P}(n) counts the number of order-preserving maps from PP to [n][n]. This function was first introduced by Richard P. Stanley in his PhD thesis, where it was also proved that it is a polynomial [26, Proposition 13.1], called the order polynomial of PP. Later, Stanley proved [27, Theorem 4.1] that the Ehrhart polynomial L⁡(𝒪⁡(P),t)L(\mathcal{O}(P),t) of 𝒪⁡(P)\mathcal{O}(P) and the order polynomial ΩP​(t)\Omega_{P}(t) of PP are related by the following:

L⁡(𝒪⁡(P),t)=ΩP​(t+1).L(\mathcal{O}(P),t)=\Omega_{P}(t+1).

Therefore, the results in this section also provide a formula to compute the Ehrhart polynomial of 𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n)\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{C}_{2n}) as an expression of Ehrhart polynomials of zigzags and prove that its coefficients are nonnegative.

We start by stating the reciprocity theorem for graded posets. Recall that a poset P=(P,⪯)P=(P,\preceq) is graded if there exists a rank function ρ:P→ℕ\rho\colon P\to\mathbb{N} such that

  1. (i)

    x≺yx\prec y implies ρ⁡(x)<ρ⁡(y)\rho(x)<\rho(y);

  2. (ii)

    if yy covers xx, then ρ⁡(y)=ρ⁡(x)+1\rho(y)=\rho(x)+1.

A graded poset PP is called rr-graded if every maximal chain of PP has length rr. For example, 𝒞2​n\mathcal{C}_{2n} and Zn+1Z_{n+1} are 11-graded posets for every n≥1n\geq 1.

Lemma 4.1.

[6, Theorem 2.3] Let P=([n],⪯)P=([n],\preceq) be an rr-graded poset. Then

ΩP​(t−r)=(−1)n​ΩP​(−t).\Omega_{P}(t-r)=(-1)^{n}\Omega_{P}(-t).

Now we can state the main result of our section. In the following proof, for a,b∈ℤa,b\in\mathbb{Z} we shall write [a,b][a,b] for the closed interval {k∈ℤ:a≤k≤b}\{k\in\mathbb{Z}\colon a\leq k\leq b\}.

Theorem 4.2.
(4.1) Ω𝒞2​n​(t)\displaystyle\Omega_{\mathcal{C}_{2n}}(t) =Ω𝒞2​n​(t−1)+n⋅ΩZ2​n−1​(t−1)+ΩZ2​n−3​(t)+∑1≤i<j≤nΩZ2​(n−j+i)−1​(t−1)⋅ΩZ2​(j−i)−1​(t)\displaystyle=\Omega_{\mathcal{C}_{2n}}(t-1)+n\cdot\Omega_{Z_{2n-1}}(t-1)+\Omega_{Z_{2n-3}}(t)+\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq n}\Omega_{Z_{2(n-j+i)-1}}(t-1)\cdot\Omega_{Z_{2(j-i)-1}}(t)
(4.2) =Ω𝒞2​n​(−t)−n⋅ΩZ2​n−1​(−t)+t⋅ΩZ2​n−3​(t)−∑1≤i<j≤n(i,j)≠(1,n)ΩZ2​(n−j+i)−1​(−t)⋅ΩZ2​(j−i)−1​(t)\displaystyle=\Omega_{\mathcal{C}_{2n}}(-t)-n\cdot\Omega_{Z_{2n-1}}(-t)+t\cdot\Omega_{Z_{2n-3}}(t)-\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq i<j\leq n\\ (i,j)\neq(1,n)\end{subarray}}\Omega_{Z_{2(n-j+i)-1}}(-t)\cdot\Omega_{Z_{2(j-i)-1}}(t)

for every n≥2n\geq 2.

ℱ4≔{f∈ℱ3:f⁡(1)=m}andℱ5≔{f∈ℱ3:f⁡(1)<m}.\mathcal{F}_{4}\coloneqq\{f\in\mathcal{F}_{3}\colon f(1)=m\}\quad\mbox{and}\quad\mathcal{F}_{5}\coloneqq\{f\in\mathcal{F}_{3}\colon f(1)<m\}.

We claim that

(4.3) ℱ5=⨆1≤i<j≤nℱi,j,\mathcal{F}_{5}=\bigsqcup_{1\leq i<j\leq n}\mathcal{F}_{i,j},

where ℱi,j={f∈ℱ5:f⁡(2​i)=f⁡(2​j)=m​ and ​f−1​(m)⊆[2​i,2​j]}.\mathcal{F}_{i,j}=\{f\in\mathcal{F}_{5}\colon f(2i)=f(2j)=m\mbox{ and }f^{-1}(m)\subseteq[2i,2j]\}. In fact, let f∈ℱ5f\in\mathcal{F}_{5}. Then f⁡(1)<mf(1)<m and there exist a<ba<b in [2​n][2n] such that f⁡(a)=f⁡(b)=mf(a)=f(b)=m. Moreover, ℱi,j∩ℱk,l=∅\mathcal{F}_{i,j}\cap\mathcal{F}_{k,l}=\emptyset if (i,j)≠(k,l)(i,j)\neq(k,l), which verifies (4.3).

Now, we can finally prove (4.1). By definition, |ℱ1|=Ω𝒞2​n​(m−1)|\mathcal{F}_{1}|=\Omega_{\mathcal{C}_{2n}}(m-1). To count the number of elements in ℱ2\mathcal{F}_{2}, let f∈ℱ2f\in\mathcal{F}_{2} be such that f⁡(a)=mf(a)=m for some a∈[2​n]a\in[2n]. Ω𝒞2​n​(t)=\displaystyle\Omega_{\mathcal{C}_{2n}}(t)= Ω𝒞2​n​(t−1)+n⋅ΩZ2​n−1​(t−1)+ΩZ2​n−3​(t)+ΩZ1​(t−1)⋅ΩZ2​n−3​(t)\displaystyle\Omega_{\mathcal{C}_{2n}}(t-1)+n\cdot\Omega_{Z_{2n-1}}(t-1)+\Omega_{Z_{2n-3}}(t)+\Omega_{Z_{1}}(t-1)\cdot\Omega_{Z_{2n-3}}(t)

(4.4) =\displaystyle= Ω𝒞2​n​(t−1)+n⋅ΩZ2​n−1​(t−1)+t⋅ΩZ2​n−3​(t)+∑1≤i<j≤n(i,j)≠(1,n)ΩZ2​(n−j+i)−1​(t−1)⋅ΩZ2​(j−i)−1​(t)\displaystyle\Omega_{\mathcal{C}_{2n}}(t-1)+n\cdot\Omega_{Z_{2n-1}}(t-1)+t\cdot\Omega_{Z_{2n-3}}(t)+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}1\leq i<j\leq n\\ (i,j)\neq(1,n)\end{subarray}}\Omega_{Z_{2(n-j+i)-1}}(t-1)\cdot\Omega_{Z_{2(j-i)-1}}(t)

where the second equality holds because ΩZ1​(t)=t\Omega_{Z_{1}}(t)=t. Equation 4.2 follows from a combination of (4.4) and Lemma 4.1. ∎

Remark 4.3.

Using a similar argument as the one used in Theorem 4.2, one can show that

ΩZn​(t)=ΩZn​(t−1)+ΩZn−2​(t)+∑1≤i≤j≤⌊n/2⌋ΩZ2​i−1​(t−1)⋅ΩZ2​j−2​i−1​(t)⋅ΩZn−2​j​(t−1),\Omega_{Z_{n}}(t)=\Omega_{Z_{n}}(t-1)+\Omega_{Z_{n-2}}(t)+\sum_{1\leq i\leq j\leq\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\Omega_{Z_{2i-1}}(t-1)\cdot\Omega_{Z_{2j-2i-1}}(t)\cdot\Omega_{Z_{n-2j}}(t-1),

where we set ΩZ−1​(t)≔1\Omega_{Z_{-1}}(t)\coloneqq 1, which is a recursive formula that does not seem to appear in the literature.

Given a polynomial p⁡(t)∈ℝ⁡[t]p(t)\in\mathbb{R}[t], let [tk]​p​(t)[t^{k}]p(t) denote the coefficient of tkt^{k} in p⁡(t)p(t).

Lemma 4.4 ([11], Page 10).

For every n≥1n\geq 1 the linear coefficient of ΩZn​(t)\Omega_{Z_{n}}(t) is given by

[t]​ΩZn​(t)=⌊n−12⌋!⋅⌈n−12⌉!n!=1n​(n−1⌊n−12⌋)−1.[t]\Omega_{Z_{n}}(t)=\frac{\lfloor\frac{n-1}{2}\rfloor!\cdot\lceil\frac{n-1}{2}\rceil!}{n!}=\frac{1}{n}\binom{n-1}{\lfloor\frac{n-1}{2}\rfloor}^{-1}\quad.

In order to prove that the order polynomial of 𝒞2​n\mathcal{C}_{2n} has nonnegative coefficients, the crucial difficulty is showing that the linear term is indeed nonnegative. Unlike the case of zigzags, which come from a skew shape, the computation of the linear term of the crown (which falls into the class of cylindric skew shapes) is more subtle and requires a complicated determinantal formula (see [11, Section 7]). By using our recursions, we can give a simpler proof of this nonnegativity:

Corollary 4.5.

For every n≥1n\geq 1 the linear coefficient of Ω𝒞2​n​(t)\Omega_{\mathcal{C}_{2n}}(t) is given by

(4.5) [t]​Ω𝒞2​n​(t)=(2​nn)−1.[t]\Omega_{\mathcal{C}_{2n}}(t)=\binom{2n}{n}^{-1}\quad.
Proof.

If n=1n=1, then Ω𝒞2​(t)=t/2+t2/2\Omega_{\mathcal{C}_{2}}(t)=t/2+t^{2}/2. Recall that ΩP​(0)=0\Omega_{P}(0)=0 if PP is a non-empty poset, that is, [1]​ΩP​(t)=0[1]\Omega_{P}(t)=0 if P≠∅P\neq\emptyset. Observe that [t]​Ω𝒞2​n​(−t)=−[t]​Ω𝒞2​n​(t)[t]\Omega_{\mathcal{C}_{2n}}(-t)=-[t]\Omega_{\mathcal{C}_{2n}}(t). Then, by (4.2), if n≥2n\geq 2,

[t]​Ω𝒞2​n​(t)\displaystyle[t]\Omega_{\mathcal{C}_{2n}}(t) =[t]​Ω𝒞2​n​(−t)−n⋅[t]​ΩZ2​n−1​(−t)⟹\displaystyle=[t]\Omega_{\mathcal{C}_{2n}}(-t)-n\cdot[t]\Omega_{Z_{2n-1}}(-t)\implies
[t]​Ω𝒞2​n​(t)\displaystyle[t]\Omega_{\mathcal{C}_{2n}}(t) =n2⋅1(2​n−1)​(2​n−2n−1)=(2​nn)−1\displaystyle=\frac{n}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{(2n-1)\binom{2n-2}{n-1}}=\binom{2n}{n}^{-1}

where Lemma 4.4 was used in the second equality. ∎

Let PP be a poset. An order ideal of PP is a subset II of PP such that if t∈It\in I and s≤ts\leq t in PP, then s∈Is\in I. Denote by J⁡(P)J(P) the distributive lattice of order ideals in PP ordered by inclusion and, if PP is finite, define the polynomial

cJ⁡(P)​(t)≔∑k≥0ck​(J⁡(P))​tk,c_{J(P)}(t)\coloneqq\sum_{k\geq 0}c_{k}(J(P))t^{k},

where ck(J(P))=|{∅=I0<I1<⋯<Ik=P}|c_{k}(J(P))=|\{\emptyset=I_{0}<I_{1}<\cdots<I_{k}=P\}|. The polynomial cJ⁡(P)​(t)c_{J(P)}(t) is known as the chain polynomial of J⁡(P)J(P).

Set

ϕ⁡(P)=∑k=1|P|(−1)k−1​ck​(J​(P))k.\phi(P)=\sum_{k=1}^{|P|}(-1)^{k-1}\frac{c_{k}(J(P))}{k}.

The following lemma is a combinatorial description of the coefficients of the order polynomial of a poset.

Lemma 4.6.

[25, Proposition 2.10] Let P=([n],⪯)P=([n],\preceq) be a poset. Then

[tk]​ΩP​(t)=1k!⋅∑∅⊊I1⊊I2⊊⋯⊊Ik=Pϕ⁡(I1)⋅ϕ⁡(I2∖I1)⋅…⋅ϕ⁡(Ik∖Ik−1).[t^{k}]\Omega_{P}(t)=\frac{1}{k!}\cdot\sum_{\emptyset\subsetneq I_{1}\subsetneq I_{2}\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq I_{k}=P}\phi(I_{1})\cdot\phi(I_{2}\setminus I_{1})\cdot\ldots\cdot\phi(I_{k}\setminus I_{k-1}).

In particular, [t]​ΩP​(t)=ϕ⁡(P).[t]\Omega_{P}(t)=\phi(P).

The importance of Lemma 4.6 is the following: given a finite poset PP, if ϕ⁡(I)≥0\phi(I)\geq 0 for every order ideal ∅≠I⊆P\emptyset\neq I\subseteq P and ϕ⁡(I∖J)≥0\phi(I\setminus J)\geq 0 for every pair ∅⊊J⊊I⊆P\emptyset\subsetneq J\subsetneq I\subseteq P, then the coefficients of ΩP​(t)\Omega_{P}(t) are nonnegative. This observation was recently rediscovered by Ferroni, Morales and Panova [11] as their Meta Theorem.

The next lemma is well-known and the proof is omitted:

Lemma 4.7.

Let PP and QQ be disjoint finite posets. Then

ΩP⊔Q​(t)=ΩP​(t)⋅ΩQ​(t).\Omega_{P\sqcup Q}(t)=\Omega_{P}(t)\cdot\Omega_{Q}(t).

Now, we have all the ingredients to prove the nonnegativity of the coefficients of Ω𝒞2​n​(t)\Omega_{\mathcal{C}_{2n}}(t):

Corollary 4.8.

[tk]​Ω𝒞2​n​(t)≥0[t^{k}]\Omega_{\mathcal{C}_{2n}}(t)\geq 0 for every k≥0k\geq 0, and every n≥1n\geq 1.

Proof.

By definition of the order polynomial, if P≠∅P\neq\emptyset, then [1]​ΩP​(t)=0[1]\Omega_{P}(t)=0, and by Corollary 4.5, [t]​Ω𝒞2​n​(t)≥0[t]\Omega_{\mathcal{C}_{2n}}(t)\geq 0. For k≥2k\geq 2, the result follows from the fact that any order ideal I∉{∅,𝒞2​n}I\not\in\{\emptyset,\mathcal{C}_{2n}\} of 𝒞2​n\mathcal{C}_{2n} is a disjoint union of zigzags, just like J∖IJ\setminus I for every pair ∅⊊I⊊J⊆𝒞2​n\emptyset\subsetneq I\subsetneq J\subseteq\mathcal{C}_{2n}. ∎

5. The h∗h^{*}-polynomial of 𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n)\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{C}_{2n})

In this section, we study the h∗h^{*}-polynomial of the order polytope 𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n)\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{C}_{2n}). We give a combinatorial interpretation for the coefficients of the h∗h^{*}-polynomial of 𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n)\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{C}_{2n}). To do this, we study a subset of alternating permutations, called cyclically alternating permutations. We will adapt the methods in [9] to the cyclically alternating case.

Let σ=σ1σ2⋯σ2​n∈S2​n\sigma=\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}\cdots\sigma_{2n}\in S_{2n} be a permutation. We say that σ\sigma is a cyclically alternating permutation if σ1<σ2>σ3<…>σ2​n−1<σ2​n>σ1\sigma_{1}<\sigma_{2}>\sigma_{3}<\ldots>\sigma_{2n-1}<\sigma_{2n}>\sigma_{1}. The set of cyclically alternating permutations on [2​n][2n] is denoted by CA2​n\operatorname{CA_{2n}}, and we set A∘​(2​n)=|CA2​n|A_{\circ}(2n)=|\operatorname{CA_{2n}}|. For more about cyclically alternating permutations, we refer to [10]. For ease of exposition, we will sometimes refer to cyclically alternating permutations as CAPs.

Definition 5.1.

For a CAP σ\sigma, we define the permutation statistic cswap⁡(σ)\operatorname{cswap}(\sigma) to be the number of i<2​ni<2n such that σ−1​(i)>σ−1​(i+1)+1\sigma^{-1}(i)>\sigma^{-1}(i+1)+1. Equivalently, it is the number of i<2​ni<2n such that ii is to the right of i+1i+1 in σ\sigma and swapping ii and i+1i+1 in σ\sigma yields a CAP.

We say that a CAP σ\sigma cyclically swaps to another CAP τ\tau when τ=σ⋅(i,i+1)\tau=\sigma\cdot(i,i+1) for some ii such that ii is to the right of i+1i+1 in σ\sigma. Note that τ\tau has one less inversion than σ\sigma. The cyclic swap set CSwap⁡(σ)\operatorname{CSwap}(\sigma) is the set of i<2​ni<2n for which we can perform a cyclic swap in σ\sigma.

Example 5.2.

For n=2n=2, then σ=2413\sigma=2413 is a CAP, σ−1=3142\sigma^{-1}=3142, cswap⁡(σ)=2\operatorname{cswap}(\sigma)=2, and CSwap⁡(σ)={1,3}\operatorname{CSwap}(\sigma)=\{1,3\}.

Remark 5.3.

The notion of cyclically swapping is the reverse notion of swapping as introduced in [9]. That is, if a CAP σ\sigma cyclically swaps to τ\tau, then τ\tau swaps to σ\sigma in the language of [9].

Given a permutation σ∈Sn\sigma\in S_{n}, Δσ\Delta^{\sigma} denotes the simplex given by the convex hull of vert⁡(σ)≔{v0σ,v1σ,…,vnσ}\operatorname{vert}(\sigma)\coloneqq\{v_{0}^{\sigma},v_{1}^{\sigma},\ldots,v_{n}^{\sigma}\}, where v0σ=∑i=1neiv_{0}^{\sigma}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}e_{i} and viσv_{i}^{\sigma} is recursively defined to be viσ=vi−1σ−eσ−1​(i)v_{i}^{\sigma}=v_{i-1}^{\sigma}-e_{\sigma^{-1}(i)}.

Proposition 5.4 (Proposition 2.12.1 [9]).

Let σ\sigma and τ\tau be alternating permutations. Then Δσ\Delta^{\sigma} intersects Δτ\Delta^{\tau} in a facet of Δσ\Delta^{\sigma} if and only if σ\sigma swaps to τ\tau or τ\tau swaps to σ\sigma.

As a result of Proposition 5.4 and Remark 5.3, we see that, for two CAPs σ\sigma and τ\tau, we have Δσ\Delta^{\sigma} intersects Δτ\Delta^{\tau} in a facet of Δσ\Delta^{\sigma} if and only if σ\sigma cyclically swaps to τ\tau or vice versa.

Let i<ji<j. We call (i,j)(i,j) an inversion of a permutation σ\sigma if σi>σj\sigma_{i}>\sigma_{j}. The inversion number of σ\sigma, denoted inv⁡(σ)\operatorname{inv}(\sigma), is the number of inversions (i,j)(i,j) of σ\sigma. Similarly, a ​n​o​n−i​n​v​e​r​s​i​o​n\emph{non-inversion} of σ\sigma is a pair (i,j)(i,j) with i<ji<j such that σi<σj\sigma_{i}<\sigma_{j}. The pair (i,j)(i,j) is called relevant if i<j−1i<j-1.

Lemma 5.5.

Let σ\sigma be a CAP. If (σ−1​(a),σ−1​(b))(\sigma^{-1}(a),\sigma^{-1}(b)) is a relevant inversion of σ\sigma, then there exists kk with b≤k<ab\leq k<a such that k∈CSwap⁡(σ)k\in\operatorname{CSwap}(\sigma).

Proof.

We proceed by induction on a−ba-b. If a−b=1a-b=1, then σ−1​(a)=σ−1​(b+1)<σ−1​(b)−1\sigma^{-1}(a)=\sigma^{-1}(b+1)<\sigma^{-1}(b)-1 gives b∈CSwap⁡(σ)b\in\operatorname{CSwap}(\sigma). So, let us assume the result true for a−b≥1a-b\geq 1 and let us prove it for a−b+1a-b+1. We look at b+1b+1 in σ\sigma. There are three possible cases:

  1. (1)

    if σ−1​(a)<σ−1​(b+1)−1\sigma^{-1}(a)<\sigma^{-1}(b+1)-1, then (σ−1​(a),σ−1​(b+1))(\sigma^{-1}(a),\sigma^{-1}(b+1)) is a relevant inversion (recall that a>b+1a>b+1). Since a−(b+1)<a−ba-(b+1)<a-b, there exists b≤b+1≤k<ab\leq b+1\leq k<a such that k∈CSwap⁡(σ)k\in\operatorname{CSwap}(\sigma) by induction;

  2. (2)

    if σ−1​(a)>σ−1​(b+1)−1\sigma^{-1}(a)>\sigma^{-1}(b+1)-1, then we claim that σ−1​(a)>σ−1​(b+1)\sigma^{-1}(a)>\sigma^{-1}(b+1). In fact, if σ−1​(a)=σ−1​(b+1)\sigma^{-1}(a)=\sigma^{-1}(b+1), then a=b+1a=b+1 , but, by hypothesis, a>b+1a>b+1. So, σ−1​(a)>σ−1​(b+1)\sigma^{-1}(a)>\sigma^{-1}(b+1), which implies σ−1​(b+1)+1≤σ−1​(a)<σ−1​(b)\sigma^{-1}(b+1)+1\leq\sigma^{-1}(a)<\sigma^{-1}(b) and gives b∈CSwap⁡(σ)b\in\operatorname{CSwap}(\sigma);

  3. (3)

    if σ−1​(a)=σ−1​(b+1)−1\sigma^{-1}(a)=\sigma^{-1}(b+1)-1, then we claim that σ−1​(b)>σ−1​(b+1)+1\sigma^{-1}(b)>\sigma^{-1}(b+1)+1. In fact, if σ−1​(b)≤σ−1​(b+1)+1\sigma^{-1}(b)\leq\sigma^{-1}(b+1)+1, then we have three cases:

    • •

      if σ−1​(b)=σ−1​(b+1)\sigma^{-1}(b)=\sigma^{-1}(b+1), then b=b+1b=b+1, since σ\sigma is a bijection, so this case cannot happen;

    • •

      if σ−1​(b)=σ−1​(b+1)+1\sigma^{-1}(b)=\sigma^{-1}(b+1)+1, then σ−1​(a)<σ−1​(b+1)<σ−1​(b)\sigma^{-1}(a)<\sigma^{-1}(b+1)<\sigma^{-1}(b), but σ−1​(a)=σ−1​(b+1)−1\sigma^{-1}(a)=\sigma^{-1}(b+1)-1 and σ−1​(b)=σ−1​(b+1)+1\sigma^{-1}(b)=\sigma^{-1}(b+1)+1 imply that a,b+1,ba,b+1,b is a decreasing consecutive sequence in σ\sigma, which contradicts that σ\sigma is a CAP;

    • •

      if σ−1​(b)<σ−1​(b+1)\sigma^{-1}(b)<\sigma^{-1}(b+1), then σ−1​(a)<σ−1​(b)<σ−1​(b+1)\sigma^{-1}(a)<\sigma^{-1}(b)<\sigma^{-1}(b+1), but σ−1​(a)=σ−1​(b+1)−1\sigma^{-1}(a)=\sigma^{-1}(b+1)-1 implies that σ−1​(a)<σ−1​(b)<σ−1​(a)+1\sigma^{-1}(a)<\sigma^{-1}(b)<\sigma^{-1}(a)+1, which is a contradiction.

    Hence, σ−1​(b)>σ−1​(b+1)+1\sigma^{-1}(b)>\sigma^{-1}(b+1)+1 and it gives b∈CSwap⁡(σ)b\in\operatorname{CSwap}(\sigma), as needed.

∎

Let σ\sigma be a cyclically alternating permutation. We define

E⁡(σ):={v:v∈vert⁡(σ)∖vert⁡(τ)​ for some CAP ​τ​ that ​σ​ cyclically swaps to}.E(\sigma):=\{v\colon v\in\vrt(\sigma)\setminus\vrt(\tau)\text{ for some CAP }\tau\text{ that }\sigma\text{ cyclically swaps to}\}.
Proposition 5.6.

A cyclically alternating permutation σ\sigma minimizes the inversion number of all cyclically alternating permutations τ\tau with E⁡(σ)⊆vert⁡(τ)E(\sigma)\subseteq\operatorname{vert}(\tau).

Proof.

Let vkσ∈vert⁡(σ)v_{k}^{\sigma}\in\operatorname{vert}(\sigma). By definition, vkσv_{k}^{\sigma} is the vector (1,…,1)(1,\ldots,1) with a 11 removed from the coordinate at the σ−1​(ℓ)\sigma^{-1}(\ell)th position for all ℓ≤k\ell\leq k. We can read off inversions (i,j)(i,j) of σ\sigma with σ⁡(j)≤k<σ⁡(i)\sigma(j)\leq k<\sigma(i) from vkσv_{k}^{\sigma} as pairs where the iith component of vkσv_{k}^{\sigma} is 11 and the jjth component is 00.

Now we claim that every relevant inversion of σ\sigma can be read from an element of E⁡(σ)E(\sigma) as above. Given a relevant inversion (i,j)(i,j) of σ\sigma, we know, by Lemma 5.5, that there exists a cyclic swap kk with σ⁡(j)≤k<σ⁡(i)\sigma(j)\leq k<\sigma(i) and (i,j)(i,j) can be read from vkσv_{k}^{\sigma}. Since kk is a cyclic swap, vkσv_{k}^{\sigma} is the opposite vertex of the intersection of Δσ\Delta^{\sigma} and Δτ\Delta^{\tau} for the CAP τ\tau that σ\sigma cyclically swaps to when swapping kk and (k+1)(k+1). Therefore, all relevant inversions of σ\sigma can be found as non-adjacent 1−01-0 pairs in a vertex in E⁡(σ)E(\sigma). This means we can count the number of relevant inversions of σ\sigma from vertices in E⁡(σ)E(\sigma). If E⁡(σ)⊆vert⁡(τ)E(\sigma)\subseteq\operatorname{vert}(\tau), then all inversions of σ\sigma are inversions in τ\tau, though τ\tau could have more. Therefore, σ\sigma minimizes inversions over all CAP τ\tau with E⁡(σ)⊆vert⁡(τ)E(\sigma)\subseteq\operatorname{vert}(\tau). ∎

Proposition 5.7.

Let σ\sigma be a cyclically alternating permutation. If σ′\sigma^{\prime} minimizes inversion number in the cyclically alternating permutations τ\tau satisfying E⁡(σ)⊆v​e​r​t​(τ)E(\sigma)\subseteq vert(\tau), then σ=σ′\sigma=\sigma^{\prime}.

Proof.

Follows from the proof of Proposition 5.6. ∎

We quickly recall the notion of a shelling. Let Λ\Lambda be the collection of maximal simplices in a pure simplicial complex of dimension dd with |Λ|=s|\Lambda|=s. An ordering Δ1,Δ2,…,Δs\Delta^{1},\Delta^{2},\ldots,\Delta^{s} on the simplices in Λ\Lambda is a shelling order if, for all 1<r≤s1<r\leq s,

⋃i=1r−1(Δi∩Δr)\bigcup_{i=1}^{r-1}(\Delta^{i}\cap\Delta^{r})

is a union of facets of Δr\Delta_{r}.

Theorem 5.8.

Let σ1,σ2,…​σA∘​(2​n)\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},\ldots\sigma_{A_{\circ}(2n)} be an ordering of the cyclically alternating permutations so that inv⁡(σi)≤inv⁡(σj)\operatorname{inv}(\sigma_{i})\leq\operatorname{inv}(\sigma_{j}) when i<ji<j. Then the associated order on Δσ1,Δσ2,…,ΔσA∘​(2​n)\Delta^{\sigma_{1}},\Delta^{\sigma_{2}},\ldots,\Delta^{\sigma_{A_{\circ}(2n)}} is a shelling order of the canonical triangulation of 𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n)\mathcal{O}({\mathcal{C}_{2n}}).

Proof.

We first show that it suffices to prove that if inv⁡(σ)≥inv⁡(τ)\operatorname{inv}(\sigma)\geq\operatorname{inv}(\tau) (that is, Δσ\Delta^{\sigma} comes after Δτ\Delta^{\tau} in the shelling order), then E⁡(σ)⊄vert⁡(τ)E(\sigma)\not\subset\operatorname{vert}(\tau). Towards this goal, let inv⁡(σ)≥inv⁡(ρ)\operatorname{inv}(\sigma)\geq\operatorname{inv}(\rho). By Proposition 5.4, Δσ∩Δρ\Delta^{\sigma}\cap\Delta^{\rho} is a facet of Δσ\Delta^{\sigma} if and only if ρ\rho swaps to σ\sigma (since ρ\rho has less inversions and a swap increases inversions by 11), which happens if and only if Δσ∩Δρ=Δσ∖{vi}\Delta^{\sigma}\cap\Delta^{\rho}=\Delta^{\sigma\setminus\{v_{i}\}} for vi∈E⁡(σ)v_{i}\in E(\sigma). If Δσ∩Δτ⊄Δσ∩Δρ\Delta^{\sigma}\cap\Delta^{\tau}\not\subset\Delta^{\sigma}\cap\Delta^{\rho} for any ρ\rho with inv⁡(σ)≥inv⁡(ρ)\operatorname{inv}(\sigma)\geq\operatorname{inv}(\rho) and Δσ∩Δρ\Delta^{\sigma}\cap\Delta^{\rho} a facet of Δσ\Delta^{\sigma}, then E⁡(σ)⊆vert⁡(τ)E(\sigma)\subseteq\operatorname{vert}(\tau). The contrapositive of this last sentence says, if E⁡(σ)⊈vert⁡(τ)E(\sigma)\not\subseteq\operatorname{vert}(\tau), then the given order is a shelling order.

If inv⁡(σ)>inv⁡(τ)\operatorname{inv}(\sigma)>\operatorname{inv}(\tau), then, since σ\sigma minimizes the inversion number over all cyclically alternating permutations that contain E⁡(σ)E(\sigma), by Proposition 5.6, we have E⁡(σ)⊄vert⁡(τ)E(\sigma)\not\subset\operatorname{vert}(\tau). If inv⁡(σ)=inv⁡(τ)\operatorname{inv}(\sigma)=\operatorname{inv}(\tau), then, by Proposition 5.7, E⁡(σ)⊄vert⁡(τ)E(\sigma)\not\subset\operatorname{vert}(\tau), because σ\sigma is the unique permutation that minimizes inversion number of all cyclically alternating permutations that contain E⁡(σ)E(\sigma). ∎

Let P=([n],⪯)P=([n],\preceq) be a poset. The Jordan–Hölder set of PP is defined as

JH(P)≔{σ=σ1σ2⋯σn∈Sn: if σi⪯σj, then i≤j for all i,j∈[n]},\operatorname{JH}(P)\coloneqq\{\sigma=\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}\cdots\sigma_{n}\in S_{n}\colon\mbox{ if }\sigma_{i}\preceq\sigma_{j},\mbox{ then }i\leq j\mbox{ for all }i,j\in[n]\},

that is, JH⁡(P)\operatorname{JH}(P) is the set of all linear extensions of PP.

The h∗h^{*}-polynomial of 𝒪⁡(P)\mathcal{O}(P) can be computed in terms of a permutation statistic on the Jordan-Hölder set of permutations. We say that a poset P=([n],⪯)P=([n],\preceq) is naturally labeled if i≺ji\prec j in PP implies i<ji<j as integers.

We say that ii is a descent of a permutation σ∈Sn\sigma\in S_{n} if σi>σi+1\sigma_{i}>\sigma_{i+1}. The descent set of σ\sigma, denoted Des⁡(σ)\operatorname{Des}(\sigma), is the set of all descents of σ\sigma. The descent number of σ\sigma, denoted des⁡(σ)\operatorname{des}(\sigma), is the number of elements of Des⁡(σ)\operatorname{Des}(\sigma).

Theorem 5.9 (Theorem 6.3.116.3.11 [2]).

Let PP be a naturally labeled poset. The h∗h^{*}-polynomial of 𝒪⁡(P)\mathcal{O}(P) is given by

h∗​(𝒪⁡(P),t)=∑σ∈JH⁡(P)tdes⁡(σ).h^{*}({\mathcal{O}(P)},t)=\sum_{\sigma\in\operatorname{JH}(P)}t^{\operatorname{des}(\sigma)}.
Theorem 5.10.

[1, Chapter 3] Let 𝔭\mathfrak{p} be a polytope with integer vertices. Let {Δ1,Δ2,…,Δs}\{\Delta^{1},\Delta^{2},\ldots,\Delta^{s}\} be a unimodular triangulation of 𝔭\mathfrak{p} using no new vertices. If {Δ1,Δ2,…,Δs}\{\Delta^{1},\Delta^{2},\ldots,\Delta^{s}\} is a shelling order, then hj∗h^{*}_{j} is the number of Δi\Delta^{i} that are added along jj of their facets in this shelling. Equivalently,

h∗​(𝔭,t)=∑i=1stai,h^{*}(\mathfrak{p},t)=\sum_{i=1}^{s}t^{a_{i}},

where ai=#⁡{k<i:Δk∩Δi​ is a facet of ​Δi}a_{i}=\#\{k<i:\Delta^{k}\cap\Delta^{i}\text{ is a facet of }\Delta^{i}\}.

Now we are ready to prove the main theorem of our section.

Theorem 5.11.

h∗​(𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n),t)=∑σ∈CA2​ntcswap⁡(σ)h^{*}(\mathcal{O}({\mathcal{C}_{2n}}),t)=\sum_{\sigma\in\operatorname{CA_{2n}}}t^{\operatorname{cswap}(\sigma)}.

Proof.

Let σ1,σ2,…​σA∘​(2​n)\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},\ldots\sigma_{A_{\circ}(2n)} be a shelling order as described in Theorem 5.8. Hence, by Proposition 5.4 and Remark 5.3, each Δσi\Delta^{\sigma_{i}} is added in the shelling along cswap⁡(σi)\operatorname{cswap}(\sigma_{i}) facets. By Theorem 5.10,

h∗​(𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n),t)=∑σ∈CA2​ntcswap⁡(σ).h^{*}(\mathcal{O}({\mathcal{C}_{2n}}),t)=\sum_{\sigma\in\operatorname{CA_{2n}}}t^{\operatorname{cswap}(\sigma)}.

∎

Theorems 5.9 and 5.11 imply the following equidistribution:

Corollary 5.12.

Let 𝒞2​n\mathcal{C}_{2n} on [2​n][2n] be naturally labeled. Then

∑σ∈CA2​ntcswap⁡(σ)=∑σ∈JH⁡(𝒞2​n)tdes⁡(σ).\sum_{\sigma\in\operatorname{CA_{2n}}}t^{\operatorname{cswap}(\sigma)}=\sum_{\sigma\in\operatorname{JH}(\mathcal{C}_{2n})}t^{\operatorname{des}(\sigma)}.
Corollary 5.13.

deg⁡(h∗​(𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n),t))=2​n−2\deg(h^{*}(\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{C}_{2n}),t))=2n-2.

Proof.

Since the only permutation τ\tau such that des⁡(τ)=2​n−1\operatorname{des}(\tau)=2n-1 is τ=(2​n,2​n−1,…,1)\tau=(2n,2n-1,\ldots,1) and such permutation does not belong to the set JH⁡(𝒞2​n)\operatorname{JH}(\mathcal{C}_{2n}), then deg⁡(h∗​(𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n),t))≤2​n−2\deg(h^{*}(\mathcal{O}({\mathcal{C}_{2n}}),t))\leq 2n-2.

Now, consider the CAP σ=(n,2​n,n−1,2​n−1,…,1,n+1)\sigma=(n,2n,n-1,2n-1,\ldots,1,n+1). Since ii is to the right of i+1i+1 for every i∈[2​n]∖{n,2​n}i\in[2n]\setminus\{n,2n\} and swapping ii and i+1i+1 yields a CAP, then cswap⁡(σ)=2​n−2\operatorname{cswap}(\sigma)=2n-2 and, hence, deg⁡(h∗​(𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n),t))≥2​n−2\deg(h^{*}(\mathcal{O}({\mathcal{C}_{2n}}),t))\geq 2n-2. ∎

Example 5.14.

and we have

∑σ∈JH⁡(𝒞2​n)tdes⁡(σ)=1+2​t+t2.\sum_{\sigma\in\operatorname{JH}(\mathcal{C}_{2n})}t^{\operatorname{des}(\sigma)}=1+2t+t^{2}.

Recall that a lattice polytope 𝔭\mathfrak{p} is called reflexive if there is an interior lattice point xx such that every facet has lattice distance one from xx. In this case, xx is the unique interior lattice point of 𝔭\mathfrak{p}. A lattice polytope is called Gorenstein if there is some r∈ℤ≥1r\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1} such that r​𝔭r\mathfrak{p} is reflexive. In this case, rr is called the index of 𝔭\mathfrak{p}. A poset is called pure if all maximal chains have the same length.

In [9], it was shown that 𝒪⁡(Zn)\mathcal{O}(Z_{n}) is a Gorenstein polytope of index 33 for every n≥1n\geq 1. We also show that 𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n)\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{C}_{2n}) is a Gorenstein polytope of index 33 for every n≥1n\geq 1 and present some consequences of this property.

Proposition 5.15.

𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n)\mathcal{O}({\mathcal{C}_{2n}}) is Gorenstein for every n≥1n\geq 1.

Proof.

By [18, §3 d], order polytopes of pure posets are Gorenstein. ∎

By [27], order polytopes admit a unimodular triangulation. This combined with Proposition 5.15 and [8, Theorem 11], gives us

Corollary 5.16.

The coefficients of the h∗h^{*}-polynomials of 𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n)\mathcal{O}({\mathcal{C}_{2n}}) are symmetric and unimodal.

Corollary 5.17.

The index of 𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n)\mathcal{O}({\mathcal{C}_{2n}}) is 33 and x=(1,2,1,2,…,1,2)x=(1,2,1,2,\ldots,1,2) is the unique interior lattice point of 3​𝒪​(𝒞2​n)3\mathcal{O}({\mathcal{C}_{2n}}).

Proof.

Let rr be the index of 𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n)\mathcal{O}({\mathcal{C}_{2n}}). By [8, Theorem 1],

(5.1) deg⁡(h∗​(𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n),t))=2​n−r+1.\deg(h^{*}(\mathcal{O}({\mathcal{C}_{2n}}),t))=2n-r+1.

Equation (5.1) combined with Corollary 5.13 imply that r=3r=3.

For the second part, observe that the facet-defining inequalities of 3​𝒪​(𝒞2​n)3\mathcal{O}({\mathcal{C}_{2n}}) are

0≤xi​ if ​i​ is odd\displaystyle 0\leq x_{i}\mbox{ if }i\mbox{ is odd}
xi≤3​ if ​i​ is even\displaystyle x_{i}\leq 3\mbox{ if }i\mbox{ is even}
x2​i−1≤x2​i​ for every ​i=1,2,…,n\displaystyle x_{2i-1}\leq x_{2i}\mbox{ for every }i=1,2,\ldots,n
x2​i+1≤x2​i​ for every ​i=0,1,…,n−1\displaystyle x_{2i+1}\leq x_{2i}\mbox{ for every }i=0,1,\ldots,n-1
x1≤x2​n,\displaystyle x_{1}\leq x_{2n},

from which it is clear that x=(1,2,1,2,…,1,2)x=(1,2,1,2,\ldots,1,2) is the unique interior lattice point of 3​𝒪​(𝒞2​n)3\mathcal{O}({\mathcal{C}_{2n}}). Moreover, xx has lattice distance 11 from each facet of 3​𝒪​(𝒞2​n)3\mathcal{O}({\mathcal{C}_{2n}}). ∎

An interesting question about h∗h^{*}-polynomials to be investigated is whether or not they have only real roots. The following conjecture was verified for 2≤n≤62\leq n\leq 6:

Conjecture 5.18.

h∗​(𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n),t)h^{*}(\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{C}_{2n}),t) is real-rooted for every n≥2n\geq 2.

5.1. The γ\gamma-nonnegativity of the h∗h^{*}-vector

Let g⁡(t)=∑i≥0gi​tig(t)=\sum_{i\geq 0}g_{i}t^{i} be a symmetric polynomial. Then, gi=gd−ig_{i}=g_{d-i} for some positive integer dd, which we define as the symmetric degree of gg.

Symmetric polynomials with symmetric degree dd span a vector space of dimension ⌊d/2⌋+1\lfloor d/2\rfloor+1. Hence, they can be written in the basis

Γd={ti​(1+t)d−2​i}i=0⌊d/2⌋,\Gamma_{d}=\{t^{i}(1+t)^{d-2i}\}_{i=0}^{\lfloor d/2\rfloor},

that is,

g⁡(t)=∑0≤2​i≤dγi​ti​(1+t)d−2​i.g(t)=\sum_{0\leq 2i\leq d}\gamma_{i}t^{i}(1+t)^{d-2i}.

The vector γ=(γ0,γ1,…,γ⌊d/2⌋)\gamma=(\gamma_{0},\gamma_{1},\ldots,\gamma_{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}) is called the γ\gamma-vector of gg and a topic of interest is the nonnegativity of the coefficients of the γ\gamma-vector of a polynomial.

The study of the nonnegativity of the γ\gamma-vector has gained significant attention due to its deep connections to combinatorics, and algebraic geometry. Initially introduced by Foata and Schützenberger [12] in the context of Eulerian polynomials and later developed further by various researchers such as Foata and Strehl [13, 14], as well as Brändén [6] and Gal [15], γ\gamma-nonnegativity emerged as a powerful concept that provides a novel approach to several important problems, particularly in combinatorics. One key area of application is in unimodality questions for symmetric polynomials. The nonnegativity of the γ\gamma-vector offers insights into the symmetric structure of a polynomial, revealing its unimodal nature and providing a potential approach for proving unimodality even for polynomials that are not real-rooted. For example, symmetric real-rooted polynomials in ℝ≥0\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} have nonnegative γ\gamma-vectors [6, Lemma 4.1]. On the other hand, every γ\gamma-nonnegative polynomial (real-rooted or not) is symmetric and unimodal. This is particularly important in combinatorics, where polynomials such as Eulerian polynomials or PP-Eulerian polynomials play a significant role in enumerating combinatorial objects (e.g., flag triangulations of spheres) and understanding combinatorial symmetries. Also, it is an interesting question finding a combinatorial interpretation of the coefficients of the γ\gamma-vector.

Let PP be a finite poset. A labeling of PP is an injection ω:P→ℤ\omega\colon P\to\mathbb{Z}. The pair (P,ω)(P,\omega) is called naturally labeled if x≤Pyx\leq_{P}y implies ω⁡(x)≤ω⁡(y)\omega(x)\leq\omega(y). In this case, ω\omega is called a natural labeling. Let (P~,ω~)(\tilde{P},\tilde{\omega}) be any canonically labeled poset [7, Page 9] obtained from (P,ω)(P,\omega) by adjoining a greatest element.

By [6, Theorem 4.2], h∗​(𝒪​(P),t)h^{*}(\mathcal{O}(P),t) has nonnegative expansion in the basis Γ|P|−r−1\Gamma_{|P|-r-1} for any sign-graded poset of rank rr, and, by [7, Theorem 6.4], the coefficients of their γ\gamma-vectors have a combinatorial interpretation. Since naturally graded posets are also sign-graded, we deduce the following:

Theorem 5.19.

For each n≥1n\geq 1, the polynomial h∗​(𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n),t)h^{*}(\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{C}_{2n}),t) has a nonnegative expansion in the basis Γ2​n−2\Gamma_{2n-2}, that is, there are nonnegative integers γ2​n,j\gamma_{2n,j} such that

h∗​(𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n),t)=∑0≤j≤n−1γ2​n,j​tj​(1+t)2​n−2−2​jh^{*}(\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{C}_{2n}),t)=\sum_{0\leq j\leq n-1}\gamma_{2n,j}t^{j}(1+t)^{2n-2-2j}

and

γ2​n,j=2−2​n+2+2​j​|{π∈JH⁡(𝒞~2​n,ω~):peak⁡(π)=j+1}|,\gamma_{2n,j}=2^{-2n+2+2j}|\{\pi\in\operatorname{JH}(\tilde{\mathcal{C}}_{2n},\tilde{\omega})\colon\peak(\pi)=j+1\}|,

where ω\omega is any natural labeling of 𝒞2​n\mathcal{C}_{2n} and peak⁡(π)=|{i:ai−1<ai>ai+1}|\peak(\pi)=|\{i\colon a_{i-1}<a_{i}>a_{i+1}\}|.

Example 5.20.

Recall that h∗​(𝒪⁡(𝒞4),t)=1+2​t+t2h^{*}(\mathcal{O}({\mathcal{C}_{4}}),t)=1+2t+t^{2}. Then,

h∗​(𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n),t)=1⋅t0​(1+t)2+0⋅t1​(1+t)0,h^{*}(\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{C}_{2n}),t)=1\cdot t^{0}(1+t)^{2}+0\cdot t^{1}(1+t)^{0},

from which follows that γ4,0=1\gamma_{4,0}=1 and γ4,1=0\gamma_{4,1}=0. By Theorem 5.19, we now verify that

|{π∈JH⁡(𝒞~4,ω~):peak⁡(π)=1}|=4|\{\pi\in\operatorname{JH}(\tilde{\mathcal{C}}_{4},\tilde{\omega})\colon\peak(\pi)=1\}|=4

and

|{π∈JH⁡(𝒞~4,ω~):peak⁡(π)=2}|=0.|\{\pi\in\operatorname{JH}(\tilde{\mathcal{C}}_{4},\tilde{\omega})\colon\peak(\pi)=2\}|=0.

In fact, a canonical labeling ω~\tilde{\omega} of 𝒞~4\tilde{\mathcal{C}}_{4} is given in Figure 9. Hence,

JH⁡(𝒞~4,ω~)={23451,23541,32451,32541}.\operatorname{JH}(\tilde{\mathcal{C}}_{4},\tilde{\omega})=\{23451,23541,32451,32541\}.

Since peak⁡(23451)=peak⁡(23541)=peak⁡(32451)=peak⁡(32541)=1\peak(23451)=\peak(23541)=\peak(32451)=\peak(32541)=1, the claim follows.

6. Open problems and further directions

We conclude this work with some open questions and further directions. One of the reasons why we studied the order polytope of the crown poset is given in this section. Recall that the ordinal sum of two posets PP and QQ, denoted by P⊕QP\oplus Q, is the poset on P∪QP\cup Q such that x≤yx\leq y in P⊕QP\oplus Q if x≤yx\leq y in PP, or if x≤yx\leq y in QQ, or if x∈Px\in P and y∈Qy\in Q. This implies

Proposition 6.1.

[16, Lemma 7.3] Let PP and QQ be finite posets. Then

𝒪⁡(P⊕Q)=conv⁡({1}Q×𝒪⁡(P)∪𝒪⁡(Q)×{0}P)⊆ℝP⊔Q.\mathcal{O}(P\oplus Q)=\conv(\{1\}^{Q}\times\mathcal{O}(P)\cup\mathcal{O}(Q)\times\{0\}^{P})\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{P\sqcup Q}.

In particular, the above proposition shows that adding a minimum or a maximum element to PP corresponds to taking a pyramid over the original order polytope. Hence, if zz is not an element of PP, then

(6.1) f⁡(𝒪⁡(z⊕P),t)=f⁡(𝒪⁡(P⊕z),t)=(1+t)​f​(𝒪⁡(P),t).f(\mathcal{O}(z\oplus P),t)=f(\mathcal{O}(P\oplus z),t)=(1+t)f(\mathcal{O}(P),t).

Let PnP_{n} be a polygon with nn vertices. Then its face lattice ℒ⁡(Pn)\mathcal{L}(P_{n}) is isomorphic to 0^⊕𝒞2​n⊕1^\hat{0}\oplus\mathcal{C}_{2n}\oplus\hat{1}. Then, by Equation (6.1), the ff-polynomial of 𝒪⁡(ℒ⁡(Pn))\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{L}(P_{n})) is given by

(6.2) f⁡(𝒪⁡(ℒ⁡(Pn)),t)=(1+t)2​f​(𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n),t).f(\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{L}(P_{n})),t)=(1+t)^{2}f(\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{C}_{2n}),t).

By [19, Theorem 1.2, Chapter 8], the product of log-concave polynomials is also log-concave. Hence, Theorem 3.12 implies

Corollary 6.2.

For all n≥2n\geq 2, the entries of the ff-vector of 𝒪⁡(ℒ⁡(Pn))\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{L}(P_{n})) form a log-concave sequence.

Moreover, Corollary 3.21 and Equation 6.2 imply

Corollary 6.3.

The coefficients of the sequence of polynomials {f⁡(𝒪⁡(ℒ⁡(Pn)),t)}n≥2\{f(\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{L}(P_{n})),t)\}_{n\geq 2} are asymptotically normal.

The order polynomial behaves well under the ordinal sum of a poset PP and an element zz not in PP:

Proposition 6.4.

Let PP be a finite poset and zz be an element not in the ground set of PP. Then

Ωz⊕P​(t)=ΩP⊕z​(t)=∑k=0|P|[ek​(P)+ek−1​(P)]​(tk),\Omega_{z\oplus P}(t)=\Omega_{P\oplus z}(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{|P|}[e_{k}(P)+e_{k-1}(P)]\binom{t}{k},

where ek​(P)e_{k}(P) is the number of order preserving surjections α:P→[k]\alpha\colon P\to[k]. In particular,

L⁡(z⊕P,t)=L⁡(P⊕z,t)=∑k=0|P|[ek​(P)+ek−1​(P)]​(t+1k).L(z\oplus P,t)=L(P\oplus z,t)=\sum_{k=0}^{|P|}[e_{k}(P)+e_{k-1}(P)]\binom{t+1}{k}.
Proof.

Consider the poset P⊕zP\oplus z and let Ek​(P⊕z)E_{k}(P\oplus z) be the set of order-preserving surjections

(6.3) α:P⊕z→[k].\alpha\colon P\oplus z\to[k].

Since zz is a maximum element of P⊕zP\oplus z, α⁡(z)=k\alpha(z)=k for every α∈Ek​(P⊕z)\alpha\in E_{k}(P\oplus z).

The set Ek​(P⊕z)E_{k}(P\oplus z) can be written as the disjoint union Ek1​(P⊕z)⊔Ek2​(P⊕z)E_{k}^{1}(P\oplus z)\sqcup E_{k}^{2}(P\oplus z), where

Ek1​(P⊕z)={α∈Ek​(P⊕z):|α−1​(k)|=1}E_{k}^{1}(P\oplus z)=\{\alpha\in E_{k}(P\oplus z)\colon|\alpha^{-1}(k)|=1\}

and

Ek2​(P⊕z)={α∈Ek​(P⊕z):|α−1​(k)|>1}.E_{k}^{2}(P\oplus z)=\{\alpha\in E_{k}(P\oplus z)\colon|\alpha^{-1}(k)|>1\}.

Since Ek1​(P⊕z)E_{k}^{1}(P\oplus z) is in bijection with Ek−1​(P)E_{k-1}(P) and Ek2​(P⊕z)E_{k}^{2}(P\oplus z) is in bijection with Ek​(P)E_{k}(P), the result follows. ∎

Unfortunately, the ordinal sum does not preserve the nonnegativity of the coefficients of the order polynomial. For example, if A⁡(4)A(4) is the antichain on 44 elements, then [t]​ΩA⁡(4)​(t)=0[t]\Omega_{A(4)}(t)=0, but [t]Ωz⊕A⁡(4)(t)=−1/30[t]\Omega_{z\oplus A(4)}(t)=-1/30.

With the help of Sage [28], it was verified that [t]Ωℒ⁡(P7)(t)=−3/1430[t]\Omega_{\mathcal{L}(P_{7})}(t)=-3/1430. However, we could not find an example of polygon PnP_{n} such that the Ehrhart polynomial of 𝒪⁡(ℒ⁡(Pn))\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{L}(P_{n})) has negative coefficients. The following question is still open:

Question 6.5.

Is 𝒪⁡(ℒ⁡(Pn))\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{L}(P_{n})) Ehrhart-nonnegative for every natural number n≥3n\geq 3?

The h∗h^{*}-polynomial of the order polytope of the ordinal sum of two finite posets, PP and QQ, is also well-known:

Theorem 6.6.

[16, Proposition 7.4]

h∗​(𝒪⁡(P⊕Q),t)=h∗​(𝒪⁡(P),t)⋅h∗​(𝒪⁡(Q),t).h^{*}(\mathcal{O}(P\oplus Q),t)=h^{*}(\mathcal{O}(P),t)\cdot h^{*}(\mathcal{O}(Q),t).

In particular, if zz is not an element of PP, then

h∗​(𝒪⁡(P),t)=h∗​(𝒪⁡(z⊕P),t)=h∗​(𝒪⁡(P⊕z),t),h^{*}(\mathcal{O}(P),t)=h^{*}(\mathcal{O}(z\oplus P),t)=h^{*}(\mathcal{O}(P\oplus z),t),

which implies

(6.4) h∗​(𝒪⁡(ℒ⁡(Pn)),t)=h∗​(𝒪⁡(𝒞2​n),t).h^{*}(\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{L}(P_{n})),t)=h^{*}(\mathcal{O}(\mathcal{C}_{2n}),t).

If PP is a poset isomorphic to the face lattice of a polytope, we call 𝒪⁡(P)\mathcal{O}(P) a polytope order polytope, or POP, for short. For polytopes of dimensions 00 (points) and 11 (line segments), their POPs are completely understood. On the other hand, Equations (6.2) and (6.4) describe the ff-polynomial and the h∗h^{*}-polynomial of POPs of 22-dimensional polytopes, so a natural question is:

Question 6.7.

How can one describe the ff-polynomial, the Ehrhart polynomial, and the h∗h^{*}-polynomial of POPs of nn-dimensional polytopes for n≥3n\geq 3?

Two natural constructions arise from the 22-dimensional case:

  1. (i)

    pyramids over polygons, and

  2. (ii)

    prisms over polygons.

In fact, the face lattice of a pyramid over a polygon PnP_{n} is isomorphic to ℒ⁡(Pn)×𝒫2\mathcal{L}(P_{n})\times\mathcal{P}_{2}, where 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2} is the chain poset on 22 elements, and the face lattice of a prism over PnP_{n} is isomorphic to

0^⊕[(ℒ⁡(Pn)∖{0^})×(ℒ⁡(S)∖{0^})],\hat{0}\oplus[(\mathcal{L}(P_{n})\setminus\{\hat{0}\})\times(\mathcal{L}(S)\setminus\{\hat{0}\})],

where SS is a line segment. Hence, a first step to studying POPs of 33-dimensional polytopes could be investigating the order polytope of the cartesian product of two posets. This sounds like a hard problem, but, since 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2} and ℒ⁡(S)\mathcal{L}(S) are posets with few elements and order relations, the following question could perhaps be more feasible:

Question 6.8.

Given a finite poset PP, how can one describe the ff-vector and the h∗h^{*}-vector of 𝒪⁡(P×𝒫2)\mathcal{O}(P\times\mathcal{P}_{2}) and 𝒪⁡(P×(ℒ⁡(S)∖{0^}))\mathcal{O}(P\times(\mathcal{L}(S)\setminus\{\hat{0}\}))?

The particular case of taking the cartesian product between a finite poset PP and the 22-chain poset 𝒫2\mathcal{P}_{2} is interesting because of the following: recall that the Boolean lattice BnB_{n} is the poset on 2[n]2^{[n]} such that A⪯BA\preceq B in BnB_{n} if A⊆BA\subseteq B. It is not hard to verify that

Bn≅𝒫2×𝒫2×⋯×𝒫2⏞n​ times.B_{n}\cong\overbrace{\mathcal{P}_{2}\times\mathcal{P}_{2}\times\cdots\times\mathcal{P}_{2}}^{n\mbox{ times}}.

An nn-simplex is an nn-dimensional polytope that is the convex hull of n+1n+1 affinely independent points, and its face lattice is isomorphic to Bn+1B_{n+1}, that is, answering Question 6.8 gives information about POPs of simplices. In particular, if the real-rootedness of h∗​(𝒪​(P),t)h^{*}(\mathcal{O}(P),t) is preserved under the cartesian product, that is, if the real-rootedness of h∗​(𝒪​(P),t)h^{*}(\mathcal{O}(P),t) implies the real-rootedness of h∗​(𝒪⁡(P×𝒫2),t)h^{*}(\mathcal{O}(P\times\mathcal{P}_{2}),t), where PP is a finite poset, then the following conjecture would be confirmed to be true:

Conjecture 6.9.

h∗​(𝒪⁡(Bn),t)h^{*}(\mathcal{O}(B_{n}),t) is real-rooted for every natural number nn.
